In [[functional analysis]], a branch of [[mathematics]], an '''operator ideal''' is a special kind of [[Class (set theory)|class]] of [[continuous linear operator]]s between [[Banach space]]s.  If an operator <math>T</math> belongs to an operator ideal <math>\mathcal{J}</math>, then for any operators <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> which can be composed with <math>T</math> as <math>BTA</math>, then <math>BTA</math> is class <math>\mathcal{J}</math> as well.  Additionally, in order for <math>\mathcal{J}</math> to be an operator ideal, it must contain the class of all finite-rank Banach space operators.

==Formal definition==

Let <math>\mathcal{L}</math> denote the class of continuous linear operators acting between arbitrary Banach spaces.  For any subclass <math>\mathcal{J}</math> of <math>\mathcal{L}</math> and any two Banach spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> over the same field <math>\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}</math>, denote by <math>\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math> the set of continuous linear operators of the form <math>T:X\to Y</math> such that <math>T \in \mathcal{J}</math>.  In this case, we say that <math>\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math> is a '''component''' of <math>\mathcal{J}</math>.  An operator ideal is a subclass <math>\mathcal{J}</math> of <math>\mathcal{L}</math>, containing every identity operator acting on a 1-dimensional Banach space, such that for any two Banach spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> over the same field <math>\mathbb{K}</math>, the following two conditions for <math>\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math> are satisfied:
:(1)  If <math>S,T\in\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math> then <math>S+T\in\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math>; and
:(2) if <math>W</math> and <math>Z</math> are Banach spaces over <math>\mathbb{K}</math> with <math>A\in\mathcal{L}(W,X)</math> and <math>B\in\mathcal{L}(Y,Z)</math>, and if <math>T\in\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math>, then <math>BTA\in\mathcal{J}(W,Z)</math>.

==Properties and examples==

Operator ideals enjoy the following nice properties.

* Every component <math>\mathcal{J}(X,Y)</math> of an operator ideal forms a linear subspace of <math>\mathcal{L}(X,Y)</math>, although in general this need not be norm-closed.
* Every operator ideal contains all finite-rank operators.  In particular, the finite-rank operators form the smallest operator ideal.
* For each operator ideal <math>\mathcal{J}</math>, every component of the form <math>\mathcal{J}(X):=\mathcal{J}(X,X)</math> forms an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] in the algebraic sense.

Furthermore, some very well-known classes are norm-closed operator ideals, i.e., operator ideals whose components are always norm-closed.  These include but are not limited to the following.

* [[Compact operator]]s
* [[Weakly compact operator]]s
* Finitely strictly singular operators
* [[Strictly singular operator]]s
* [[Completely continuous operator]]s

==References==
* Pietsch, Albrecht: ''Operator Ideals'', Volume 16 of ''Mathematische Monographien'', Deutscher Verlag d. Wiss., VEB, 1978.
